summary_html: Child safely **reunified with parent or guardian**, case closed. Federal policy treats reunification as the preferred outcome once risk factors are mitigated.
authority_html:
- **Adoption and Safe Families Act (ASFA)** — establishes reunification timelines and permanency goals  
- **SSA Title IV-E (42 U.S.C. §§ 670–679c)** — funds reunification services and tracks permanency outcomes

case_law.method: v1.1.0 case-law rebuild: authorities selected per decision point, each opinion retrieved from CourtListener and read; holding and quote taken from the opinion text; independently re-verified before release. Previous keyword-matched Justia listings were removed.

key_cases.holding: Except for narrowly defined statutory exceptions the state must have made reasonable efforts to reunify the family before parental rights are terminated, but the specific R.C. 2151.419(A)(1) reasonable-efforts determination applies only at the enumerated removal and disposition hearings and not at a hearing on an R.C. 2151.413 permanent-custody motion, where the agency must prove reasonable efforts only if it has not already done so.
key_cases.relevance: Reunification is the outcome the reasonable-efforts requirement exists to pursue.
key_cases.quote: we hold that, except for a few narrowly defined exceptions, the state must have made reasonable efforts to reunify the family prior to the termination of parental rights

key_cases.holding: The statutory sunset date does not automatically divest a juvenile court of jurisdiction, but where the problems that gave rise to the original complaint have been resolved or sufficiently mitigated the court may not enter further dispositional orders on that complaint.
key_cases.relevance: Once the conditions that caused removal are corrected, the court loses the basis for continued orders and the case must move toward return home.
key_cases.quote: Where the original problems have been resolved or sufficiently mitigated, courts may not make further dispositional orders based on the original complaint.

key_cases.holding: An order that denies the agency's motion for permanent custody, terminates the agency's temporary custody and awards legal custody to a parent is a final, appealable order under R.C. 2505.02 because it affects the substantial rights of the parties and ends the proceeding.
key_cases.relevance: An award of legal custody back to a parent is the reunification disposition the Court treats as final and appealable.
key_cases.quote: In contrast, a parent does have a substantial right in the custody of his or her child.

key_cases.holding: A juvenile court may not find that a child cannot or should not be placed with either parent unless it finds by clear and convincing evidence that at least one of the then eight enumerated R.C. 2151.414(E) factors exists; general concerns outside the list will not do.
key_cases.relevance: Where no enumerated factor is proved, the statute presumes the child can be returned within a reasonable time.
key_cases.quote: permanent custody may not be granted unless the trial court finds clear and convincing evidence that one or more of the eight enumerated factors in R.C. 2151.414(E) exist

key_cases.holding: An agency may move for permanent custody on the R.C. 2151.414(B)(1)(d) '12 of 22' ground only if the child had already been in agency temporary custody for twelve of a consecutive twenty-two-month period when the motion was filed; time between filing and the hearing does not count, and a juvenile court lacks authority to grant the motion on that ground otherwise.
key_cases.relevance: It protects the reunification window by refusing to let the months between the filing of the motion and the hearing count toward the statutory period.
key_cases.quote: an agency must afford parents the full 12-month period to work toward reunification before moving for permanent custody on R.C. 2151.414(B)(1)(d) grounds

key_cases.holding: Former R.C. 2151.413(A) required a children services agency to have had current temporary custody of the child for at least six months immediately preceding the filing of a motion for permanent custody, and because the agency had not, the trial court had no authority to grant permanent custody.
key_cases.relevance: The waiting period exists to give parents a final chance at reunification, and the Court held that an agency may not bypass it by relying on an earlier, non-continuous period of custody.
key_cases.quote: we believe that given the seriousness of permanently divesting a parent of the right to raise a child, the procedural requirements of former R.C. 2151.413(A) should be strictly construed

timeline_requirements.starts_from: Child enters agency temporary custody — the earlier of adjudication under Ohio Rev. Code § 2151.28 or 60 days after removal from home
timeline_requirements.consequence_of_miss: Not stated in the statute; the agency with custody must file the permanent custody motion unless an exception in Ohio Rev. Code § 2151.413(D)(3) applies
